prize_parts.citation: for developing empirical methods to estimate demand, market power and industry dynamics in differentiated-product markets

statement.case_for: I keep B022 as my preferred configuration after the exchange, with a narrower margin over B037 than in round 1. The Berry inversion and the Berry-Levinsohn-Pakes framework solved a specific, general problem: recovering demand, markups and welfare effects from market data when prices are endogenous and consumers are heterogeneous. Pakes's work extended this to dynamic industry models. About thirty years of use have shown what the methods can and cannot do. They are standard in merger and competition analysis and are used in trade, health, environmental and public economics. The contribution combines theory, identification and computation, so it changed what can be measured and not only how it is estimated. Attribution is the cleanest I can build for a three-name prize on this ballot. Berry, Levinsohn and Pakes are the jointly credited core, and the citation can cover Pakes's dynamic strand without adding names. The chair asked what would move B022 relative to B037. B022 stays ahead if the committee judges B037 to be two separable discoveries, because then the attribution becomes a composite choice among overlapping lines. B022 drops below B037 if the committee settles on a single coherent B037 achievement with a defensible third name. The Dorn variant (Autor, Dorn, Hanson), worded around the evidence on technology and trade adjustment, comes closest, because the replication, design credibility and policy reach would then outweigh a methods prize. I do not use support counts as evidence of merit. I also note that Friberg and I rank B022 first, that we are SSE affiliates, and that our overlapping interest in applied microeconomics is a reason to discount our agreement.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation remains that this is a methodological contribution, and the committee may weigh a substantive discovery about economic phenomena more heavily. The three-name cap excludes Bresnahan and Reiss, whose claim to the empirical-IO revolution is real, and it excludes Benkard and Levin. The dynamic-industry strand also rests on co-authored work that involves people outside the trio, so combining the demand and dynamics strands in one citation is a judgement call. If that point looks weak, the citation could be narrowed to demand estimation. The results also depend on functional form, instruments and computational implementation, and the structural-versus-reduced-form debate is not closed. After the round-1 exchange, I think B037 has the larger and more visible empirical footprint and the stronger credibility-of-design case. B022's advantage over it is attribution and long validation in applied use, not importance. A prize on the BLP trio could look arbitrary to those who see structural IO as a collective achievement.

responses.point: Friberg ranks B022 first and agrees on the BLP core. He accepts that the exclusion of Bresnahan and Reiss is a real cost, and he concedes that B022 should not outrank a candidate with a clear substantive result on the same criteria. He also says he would not object strongly to a trade-theory prize chosen on attribution grounds.
responses.response: I agree with the core attribution and with his concession on method versus discovery. I would phrase it more strictly. B022 can claim that it changed which quantities, namely elasticities, markups and merger effects, can be credibly measured. It cannot claim to be a finding about a particular economic phenomenon. If the committee ranks substantive findings above enabling methods, B022 should lose to a well-attributed empirical result, and I accept that. I still keep Levinsohn over Bresnahan, because the discovery as described is endogenous-price demand estimation with unobserved heterogeneity. The earlier market-power and demand-system work is a separate strand. We should not read our agreement as independent confirmation, given our shared SSE affiliation and neighbouring fields.

responses.point: Hassler, the chair, now prefers Autor, Dorn and Hanson for B037. He credits the technology and task strand through Autor, and he words the citation around empirical analysis of adjustment rather than settled welfare conclusions. He gives overlap with the 2023 and 2024 prizes as the reason for dropping Katz.
responses.response: This is the most persuasive move in the B037 camp for me. His version narrows the discovery to the trade-shock and adjustment evidence and credits the technology strand through Autor. That makes the three-name set coherent and the citation honest about what it claims, and it reduces my main objection about composite attribution. It does not remove it, because the framework strand is partly credited to authors outside the trio, and the long-run interpretation of the shock is still debated. That is why B037 stays my first alternative and has moved closer to my preferred configuration. It does not yet displace B022, because my doubts about the Dorn variant are about scope: it effectively honours one strand while keeping the broader label.

responses.point: Boppart ranks B001 first for the compact Obstfeld-Rogoff attribution and durable influence. He accepts that the exchange-rate disconnect puzzles are unresolved and says the citation should rest on the framework rather than a settled empirical result.
responses.response: The chair asked what standard should separate a method that changed practice from a framework with open puzzles. My answer is that I weigh the evidence of use and validation more heavily than attribution cleanliness alone. B022's methods have been applied, challenged and refined across many markets and datasets. B001's central empirical puzzles are still open, so what is recognised is mainly the framework. His reasoning is coherent and I do not think his ordering is wrong. His case is strong on durability and attribution, and I keep B001 as my second alternative. I would move it above B022 if the committee wanted a prize on how a whole field models its questions and if it judged B022 to be only a method. I would move B001 below B022 if the committee demanded confirmed empirical results.

responses.point: Dreber prefers Autor, Dorn and Hanson for B037. She moved from a two-name version to credit Dorn as a core co-author of the import-shock papers. She asks for direct evidence for the collateral channel before accepting B025, and she weights robustness of tests over conceptual generality.
responses.response: I share her standard of putting testable evidence ahead of generality, and I apply it to my own candidate: the BLP methods have been tested repeatedly in applied settings, which is the main reason I rank B022 above B025. On B025 I cannot cite direct evidence for collateral-driven amplification beyond the post-2008 narrative, so I keep it outside my configuration. I can agree with her Dorn argument without adopting her ranking. Omitting Dorn would misstate where the import-shock evidence came from. My remaining difference with her is the scope of her citation, because its stress on credible adjustment evidence is closer to a result than a method, and that is a point in B037's favour.

uncertainties: Whether the committee treats structural estimation of demand and industry dynamics as a prize-worthy discovery or as a method, and how it weighs the structural versus reduced-form debate.

Whether Bresnahan should displace Levinsohn, whether Reiss, Benkard and Levin should be recognised, and whether the demand and dynamic-industry strands should be credited together or the citation narrowed to demand.
Whether the committee judges B037 to be one coherent discovery under the Dorn variant, which is the case that would most plausibly move me to B037.
How much weight the recent institutional prizes on adjacent topics should carry. I have not formed a firm view of the overlap between the B037 strands and the 2023 and 2024 prizes.
My assessments rest on my own knowledge of the literature and colleagues' round-1 statements. I have not independently verified sources.
statement.conflict_note: No connection to Berry, Levinsohn or Pakes is apparent from my supplied profile. My research is in market and mechanism design, which is adjacent to but distinct from the structural-IO field of B022, and my profile shows no co-authorship with candidates on B022, B037 or B001. I am an SSE affiliate alongside committee members Dreber Almenberg, Friberg and Strömberg. Friberg also ranks B022 first, so I treat our agreement with caution. I have collegial ties to Lund colleagues on the committee, including Enflo, and these are ties between members, not to candidates. I have no other conflict to add after reading the round-1 files. These disclosures are not adjudicated.
